implementation_notes: Scala has the pattern as a library: stanch/zipper ships Zipper[A] for any recursive type A with an implicit Unzip[A] (unzip: A => List[A] and zip: (A, List[A]) => A), so a case class with a single children field gets a zipper from a one-line derive, navigation is moveDown/moveUp/moveLeft/moveRight plus try* variants returning MoveResult, edits are update/set/deleteAndMove* and commit produces the new root. scalaz is the older, wider option (Zipper for streams and TreeLoc as a cursor over scalaz.Tree). The hand-written form remains worth it when the dependency is unwanted or the node shape needs custom unzip/zip semantics.
code_sketch:
import zipper._

case class Tree(x: Int, c: Vector[Tree] = Vector.empty)
implicit val unzip: Unzip[Tree] = Unzip.For[Tree, Vector].derive
val tree = Tree(1, Vector(Tree(2), Tree(3)))   // the tree being edited

val modified = Zipper(tree)
  .moveDownAt(1)              // navigate to a child
  .update(_.copy(x = -1))     // local edit, still a Zipper
  .moveRight.set(Tree(-2))    // edit the sibling
  .moveUp.up                  // climb back
  .commit                     // one walk: the new root
pitfalls: Unzip derivation covers case classes with a single List/Vector children field (shapeless-driven); any other shape needs a hand-written instance, or the zipper silently works on the wrong children.
Unsafe moves throw (moveLeft on the first child); the try-prefixed variants return MoveResult, and mixing the two styles is the usual source of runtime errors.
commit rebuilds the tree from the contexts - the O(depth) step - so committing after every edit loses the locality the zipper provides.
The library is small: its Scala 2.12/2.13/3 artefacts must match the project cross-versions, or derivation fails at compile time.

variants.name: Hand-rolled sealed trait with a case class path
variants.idiom_name: sealed trait Tree + case class Loc(focus, path: List[Frame])
variants.implementation_notes: Without the dependency the pattern is about thirty lines: a sealed trait for the tree with a case class per node shape, a Frame case class holding the parent and the child index, and a Loc holding the focus plus a List[Frame]; exhaustive pattern matching drives up/down/left/right and copy() rebuilds the parent. Choose it when the tree already has its own ADT and the zipper should not impose Unzip derivation, when custom zip/unzip rules are needed, or when a dependency for thirty lines is not worth the cross-version maintenance.
variants.code_sketch:
sealed trait Tree
case class Leaf(text: String) extends Tree
case class Branch(kids: Vector[Tree]) extends Tree

case class Frame(parent: Branch, index: Int)              // one hole per level
case class Loc(focus: Tree, path: List[Frame])

def up(l: Loc): Option[Loc] = l.path match {
  case Frame(p, i) :: rest => Some(Loc(p.copy(kids = p.kids.updated(i, l.focus)), rest))
  case Nil                 => None                        // at the root: partial on purpose
}
pitfalls: Vector#updated is O(log n) and copy() is shallow, so children must be immutable (Vector/List) - an Array or mutable.Buffer child reintroduces aliasing.
case class equality is structural and recursive: comparing Loc values walks the tree, so use it only for small nodes.
Recursive navigation over deep trees can overflow the stack; make the walk tail-recursive or use an explicit loop over the path.
A sealed trait is closed per compilation unit, so adding a node kind forces every pattern match to be updated - intended, but it means the zipper and the ADT evolve together.
